The whole time you're hyper aware of media presentation, bias, circumstance vs connection, reading tone from digital content, privacy vs security (what IS safety?), oh yeah and the fact that you're accessing information and content that's CLEARLY supposed to be private. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is pretty much police state simulator 2016. You play as an investigator spying on citizens of The Nation to maintain peace and order for the state.

The gameplay consists of reading articles, profiles, text messages, emails etc and clicking on highlighted text. Sounds pretty lame but who knew clicking on highlighted text could be so addictive? By reading various bits of info you piece together the overarching story and you ruin careers, make arrests and generally be an authoritarian douchebag. Or you can flout the rules and share incorrect information and be a bit of a rebel.

Said story is where the game really shines. As you're prying in to peoples private lives you begin to actually care about them and their troubles, and finding out what happens to to them is one of the things driving you on to the end. While spying on the various characters in the game you'll also read articles about current events, fleshing out the world and The Nation's history. The games central mystery unfolds in a satisfying way with plenty of (sometimes predictable) twists and turns along the way.

I finished my first playthrough by being a good little government lackey, taking pride in the fact that everyone hated my devotion to the state and making sure I crushed my enemies. I suppose next time I'll be a terrori- uh, political activist. I particularly enjoyed getting moaned at by my superiors for collecting pointless information such as favourite colours and foods.

I enjoyed the games soundtrack too, although to be fair its mainly all just ambience.

My only real criticisms of the game are it's quite short (7ish hours - although there's things you can do differently allowing multiple playthroughs), and I would've have liked more opportunities to be a sinister government agent, though as it's a story based game I can't knock the devs too harshly for that. 

In summary: If you want a short, simple game with a good story and multiple endings you can't go wrong with Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You.
It's like Simulacra and Welcome to the Game made love and created this materpiece.

Orwell resembles Hypnospace Outlaw with a lens of ripped-from-the-headlines political thrills rather than the bittersweet memories of a technology that has since gone disastrously wrong. 

It enables you to indulge your voyeuristic urges and piece together a mystery through evidence gathering, inductive reasoning, and plain ol' guessing at what the authors intended. The sleek UI, maybe-too-obvious musical stings, and actually-pretty-well-constructed material surrounding the central mystery, all help spark the player's curiosity. That, combined with a ongoing series of unfolding conspiracies, creates a whodunit that is, at minimum, passable. 

The two major strikes against this game are its UI and its actual writing. 

You need to juggle a web browser, a list of wiretapped communications, and a list of hacked computers, and the conversations progress at a quasi-real-time (read: agonizingly slow) pace. It doesn't ruin the game, but it does make certain points a slog. 

The writing is...meh. The dialogue feels rather stilted in places, particularly during more emotionally-charged moments. Moreover, the handful of red herrings that the game throws at you are really damn obvious if you've ever seen a social media feed. I didn't predict every single plot development that the game threw at me, but the attempts at misdirection felt more like they were thrown in by obligation more than anything else. 

These don't ruin the game; however, I wouldn't play the game again anytime soon. 

I paid about 3 bucks for about 4 hours of a decent game and an opportunity to explore a nice little plot, wrapped in mediocre dialogue and menu navigation. It was definitely worth the price of entry. I wouldn't necessarily regret paying full price for the experience, but at that point its value becomes far more subjective. 

If you're jonesing for a game that lets you be in control of the global surveillance machine, you could do far worse.

However, very early on I've run into a bug where I can't continue the game any further and a message stating "Find out Cassandra's attitude towards the assault or violence in general" is stuck on the top of the screen. After investigating I found a forum post from 2016 where the developer was talking about the problem, meaning the developer has neglected fixing this bug after four years. I have restarted and verified my game files but I still can't continue past this point. It's unfortunate to see this issue persist in such an intriguing game that I was enjoying so much but now will have to submit for a refund.

This game is huge disappointment.  The authors are clearly not up to date on the current status of surveillance in the United States today.  The work this game depicts that your character does, is hopelessly antiquated, it is how this was done 20 years ago.  If you have read any of the follow up reporting on all of the information Edward Snowden released, you know almost all of this is automated and much more pervasive.  This is nothing more than a really tedious drag and drop version of "Papers Please" with a pretty pastel GUI.

This game delivers on the concept of the surveillance apparatus. It is interesting to watch the connections develop between people, and consider how broadly one investigation bring in many aspects of people's lives. I liked scrolling through the alternate social media sites and doing some detective work to pick the more credible information. Building in context on the suspects was fun!
I did have some trouble with the game mechanic. It is sometimes difficult to understand when a piece of information is important for the game to progress. If you want to err on the side of protecting privacy, this can stymie you. I suppose this fits within the mindset of the investigator, though. The game helpfully highlights pages with relevant information: it took me a long time to get the hang of that. If a page is highlighted, it really does mean you have overlooked something! You really depend on this mechanic because there are not that many walkthroughs for this game if you are stuck. I got badly stuck 4 times.

TBH, the only reason I finally ended up playing this game over everything else in my backlog was because Gabe Newell said in an interview that he really liked the game.

I liked it too.  I would put the genre closest to this game as a "choose your own adventure" Visual Novel, but without a lot of the VN tropes.

To complete the game is about 5-6 hours. You serve the role as "investigator" and find information on suspects involved in crimes.  Another government official makes arrest decisions based on the information that you choose to (or not to) give him.  You cannot directly communicate with this official, only send him certain pieces of information.

This creates an interesting dynamic. You can present misleading evidence to get people arrested, or you can try to protect those who you think are not troublemakers. You feel like you have a lot of power, but at the same time, you'll often have information misinterpreted. A complaint that I have is that sometimes, certain pieces of information seem completely irrelevant, but are needed to be sent to progress the story. At some points I just found myself essentially uploading everything to make the plot advance.

At certain points in the game you'll be given a choice between 2 conflicting pieces of evidence, where you can only upload one. Sometimes, it was completely unclear which evidence was the "truth". However, other times, I was able to take a logical guess as to what was correct based on other information I had found.

Supposedly, there are multiple endings based on the decisions you make (I have not replayed the game yet). I elected to NOT savescum to get the most desirable outcome (though I think my run was mostly clean), and I highly suggest you don't either. Believe me, it's more !!!FUN!!! that way.

As a whole, it's a very good game with a couple of flaws. Worth buying on a sale. Probably not worth full price unless this type of game interests you.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

An interesting title. It's essentially a simulation of what it would be like to work as an impartial agent for a foreign government, spying for them, gathering data and sharing it with your adviser so that they can make decisions about who is a suspect and attempt to stop them. This basically all takes place from your character's computer screen.

In essence, the plot revolves around you, the "investigator", being tasked with finding out who is responsible for a recent bombing in a public place within "The Nation" (the country that runs this Orwellian nightmare). The first chapter is basically the tutorial, but don't let that fool you into believing your choices don't matter.

EVERY piece of data you choose to share can be used by the "adviser" (a partner who can speak to and advise you but you can never speak to yourself) to make decisions about what to do next. If you, say, take words out of context, you can get someone arrested for nothing at all. Then again, maybe that's worth it (do the ends justify the means?) to stop a terrorist bombing. This game is basically a series of choices. You won't always have much time to act. Most of the time you're given free reign and only after tossing in specific information are you able to advance, but it works together pretty well. Once you beat the game, you're likely to want to replay chapters to fix details you messed up, causing an unexpected result. I often find I mess up more than once (I've played more than 6 hours, but I haven't seen every result) and, somewhat frustratingly, have to do the whole chapter over again just to get back to that point and fix it, but it's not so bad. If you approach the game as an "I'll try my best and live with the consequences" sort of thing, the end result could be pretty amazing. I highly recommend that at least for your first playthrough.

Don't fret over mistakes. Try your best.

And if you like the idea of being what basically amounts to a spy in the IT department, you'll probably enjoy this game. The sequel isn't quite as incredible, but that's mostly because it isn't really a sequel. I think it takes part along the same story which doesn't make much sense because I always got the impression you were the only team using Orwell. I think the developers just wanted to make another game and couldn't justify it properly. It's alright. I would still suggest playing the sequel after just because it's a fun concept and the developers deserve the support. They worked hard on this and it very clearly shows. Good concept, good aesthetic design, interesting story. It's a mystery you can unravel for yourself and it's a damn enjoyable one at that. Please, sincerely, give it a try if this sounds at all enticing.

It's not an immensely long game (probably about 6 hours for your first time through), but that by no means makes it less worthwhile.

It doesn't overstay its welcome and delivers a satisfying experience.

The game starts very simply:
There was a terror attack, and it’s up to you to investigate all available sources to discover who is responsible.
Basically detective work in the 21st century.
But as the game progresses, you discover there is much more than meets the eye.
Not only the suspects you track, their actions and relationships, but also your actions, and those of your superiors, all become important.
You start off as a mere spectator, but even by witnessing the events, you are already impacting them.
And once you realize your impact on the world you were meant to observe, you’re now faced with difficult choices.
Choices that are not right or wrong - only choices you need live with for the rest of your life…

This is a really good game, that dives deep into questions of terror, accountability, privacy, and more.

The only issue I had with this game, is that even though you don’t have to submit every single piece of evidence you find.
And can be even reprimanded for submitting irrelevant evidence,
The game simply refuses to progress until you submit almost every piece.
For example:
Let’s say you discover a person likes strawberry ice cream. But that has nothing to do with determining if he’s a terrorist or not, so you ignore this piece of info (mark it as ignored).
Then nothing happens. The game simply refuses to progress any further.
So you submit the only remaining piece of info, that the suspect likes strawberry ice cream, and like clockwork, you’re immediately reprimanded by your superior that this piece of data has nothing to do with the case at hand (daaa….).
But then suddenly the suspect receives an incriminating phone call - and the game suddenly starts progressing.

So instead of submitting useless data being a trigger to game progression, simply marking the data as “ignored” should serve the same purpose.

Other than that - it’s a really good game.
Much better than it’s sequel (Ignorance is Strength)

I usually don't like games with lots of reading. The exception to that rule is this game. The narrative being told from the view of the spy software Orwell with the player being the investigator using the tool, playing middleman between the AI and what actually gets processed, is a great twist to how visual novels usually work.

The game's interface, while relatively simple, but maybe a bit cluttered, is very easy to use while still giving the player tools to not get lost between sources of information, marking sources with new information, sources with unsubmitted "data chunks" and sources with disabled (marked by the player as not important or false information) "data chunks" with icons.

The artstyle is is unique and definitely detailed enough to get a good picture of the people involved in the story. The OST does its job very well and never got boring to me, even after multiple playthroughs, rare sound effects help convey the impact of situations very well.

Usually I only end up 100%ing games I like. I have long ago gotten 100% Achievements in this game and now just revisited it and enjoyed my latest playthrough.

The Linux version runs quite well but seems to have some graphical glitches at least on my system (intel i5-6600k, GTX970 with nvidia driver 435 on Kubuntu). Switching to the windows version using Steam Proton (I used gloriuseggroll's custom proton 5.4, but a user on protondb also had success with official proton 4.11) fixed these issues, while even keeping my save files, which is definitely a first.

A short, but very interesting, unpredictable storyline with fleshed-out characters. The game is entirely about decision-making, and is essentially point & click, but is nonetheless enjoyable. Get it for like 2 quid.

Something I find interesting about the players' comments on this game is: 
Almost all comments in English are positive, while players from other countries are more likely to find the story disputable. The question is that should we forgive a terrorist that murdered innocents in the name of "privacy" or "freedom"?  Is our privacy a price too high to take for national security? While these questions are arguable enough, the game has its own tendency of siding with Juliet and overthrow the ORWELL. But making the opposite decision doesn't necessarily mean "2+2=5". Unlike 1984, we don't torture people for holding different opinions; we don't spy on people wherever they go;   All we concern is to make sure that the criminal doesn't leave unpunished by the law.

It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.

Honestly this game isn't Orwellian, its more Snowdenian? In that there's no actual dystopian totalitarian state, rather a look at what "real", modern state surveillance systems may be like behind the scenes.
